q: Just because you are angry at your boss, don't *transfer your anger to* us.
You can leave now. *The coast is clear*.
o: No one is watching to stop you.
The weather is very bad, so you must
e: smuggling or contraband.

q: Someone else volunteered for the extra duty. You're *off the hook*.
e: free If a fish is hooked, he is in big trouble. If the fish is *off the hook*, he has managed to escape and he is now free.

q: This new office furniture *fits the bill*.
e: If something fits the bill, it is perfect. It's just what you want and need. It meets your needs exactly.

q: Athletes who want to be bouncers in clubs and bars are *a dime a dozen*.
e: be a dime a dozen *us* ( *UK also* be two/ten a penny ) to be common and/or of very little value . Books like this are a dime a dozen.

q: We were sitting there eating lunch when suddenly Craig *took a powder*.
o: He stole some of my good.
e: take a powder leave quickly; to run away or disappear

q: I'll try to *keep them at bay* while you get away.
e: hold/keep sth/sb at bay : to hinder or to prevent someone or something unpleasant Exercise can help keep fat at bay.

q: I think this is *a red herring*.
e: ˌred herring: a fact, idea or subject that takes people's attention away from the central our attention away from the truth.

q: Craig got his next assignment. He'll be *in the boondocks* for three years.
o: in an enviable place that the rest of us
e: *The boondocks* is a very remote, primitive area far from big cities. There are no cultural amenities within hundreds of miles.

q: The unit operates _______ the direct control of the joint headquarters.
e: 'Under the control/command of' is the fixed expression.

q: The entire meal, including drinks and tip, *amounted to* $512.
e: *Amount to* = *come to* (add up to a total): The bill came to $512.

q: The movie was *terribly good*.
e: *Terribly* = *awfully*, extremely, quite, very (The key word here is "good," not "terrible.")

q: My uncle deals in *real estate*.
e: *Real estate* = land and property, buildings

q: He is leaving here *for good*.
e: *For good* = forever, for always

q: My younger brothers fight each other all the time, but I refuse to *be partisan*.
e: *Take sides* = be partisan = show favoritism for one side over the other = not being neutral

q: Let's *stop working on* this exercise for a minute and do something different.
e: *Put aside* = move something to the side and not work with it for a while

q: The next test will be *a piece of cake*.
e: *A piece of cake* = something very simple, easy to do

q: Can you finish the job by tomorrow? - *no sweat*.
e: *No sweat* = It will be so easy that we won't even sweat.

q: I can't go to the movies with you. I have to *burn the midnight oil*.
e: *Burn the midnight oil* = work or study late into the night.

q: He's *full of beans*.
e: *Full of beans* = wrong = doesn't know what he's talking about = *full of hot air* = incorrect about things

q: My neighbor drives *like a bat out of hell*.
e: *A bat out of hell*= fast, wild, crazy, dangerous

q: It's time for us to *talk turkey*.
e: to talk turkey = to talk seriously about something important

q: Look at Craig. He's typing *up a storm*, isn't he?
e: to do anything *up a storm* means to do it very hard, very seriously, working much job at hand.

q: He's *plying a new trade* these days.
o: He is driving a new car.
He is living in a different home.
e: A *trade* = a job. To *ply a trade* = to work at a job.

q: The *bean counters* probably won't agree to your budget requests.
o: accountants or clerks in a business
coaches or trainers for very weak athletes
e: *Bean counter* (informal, slightly negative) = an accountant or finance official who cares mainly about costs.

q: After a couple of beers, Craig started *spilling his guts*.
o: asking to be served a lot of good
e: to spill your guts = to tell all of your secrets to confess a lot of serious things

q: I made a *serious error* on the math test.
e: error = mistake = wrong answer serious = big = major

q: *It's a shame* that Capt. Whitfield got kicked out of school for plagiarizing someone's theme.
e: shame = bad =disgraceful = not good

q: Craig *catches on* really fast, doesn't he?
e: two-word verb *to catch on* = to learn, to understand, to comprehend

q: *I ran into* an old friend of mine at Fairview Mall.
e: *To run into* = *meet by chance*

q: *I sent for* Mariah Carey's new CD.
e: *Send for* = to order something through the mail system

q: The Police are *searching for* clues.
e: *Look for* = search for = try to find = seek

q: You have to *search for* that word in the dictionary.
e: *Look up* = search for in a book, try to find in a book

q: *Be careful*! You almost stepped on that snake.
e: *Look out* = watch out = be careful = pay attention = be careful

q: I wonder how they *invented the idea for* The Matrix.
e: *Think up* = to invent = create = make up

q: The tour guide *called our attention to* a lot of old buildings.
e: *Point out* = call attention to = tell people about = show = demonstrate

q: It's very cold. You might want to *continue wearing your jacket*.
e: *Keep on* = continue wearing an item of clothing. Keep your hat on. We're going right back outside.

q: He *is a candidate for* promotion this month.
e: *To be up for* = to be a candidate for advancement She is up for soldier of the quarter, and she'll probably get it.

q: I have too much work already. I can't *accept the responsibility for* any more.
e: *Take on* = to accept the responsibility for more work or for more duties

q: My brother is *late in* paying his bills.
e: *To be behind in* = to be late in doing something

q: Some prisoners have to *subsist on* nothing but bread and water for months.
e: *Live on* = to survive on. You live on food. You live on a certain amount of money per month.

q: Blake *registered at* the hotel at 3:30.
e: *Check in* = to register = to sign in You check in at the airline counter at the airport at a hotel at a new military base

q: When you go to Kansas City, *try to find my cousin and visit him*.
e: *Look up* a person = try to find and visit him = get in touch with = locate

q: We Can't *remain at an equal pace with* that car. It's too fast.
e: *Keep up with* = maintain the same speed as someone or something else.

q: You want to get married? Please *consider your decision very carefully*.
e: to think something through = to consider it carefully, to weigh all the options

q: Someone has been *snooping into* your private life. Do you know who and why?
e: to snoop = to pry into = to

q: Some people say President Grant was *crooked*.
e: *Crooked* = not straight = slang for dishonest

q: The captured soldier _____.
e: This is a fixed expression: to commit suicide

q: When I neared home, I could see that my neighbor's house was_____ fire.
e: fixed expression *on* fire

q: Be careful! You are _____ danger if you don't leave now.
e: fixed expression to be *in* danger. Opposite: out of danger

q: Report to the Major _____ once!
e: fixed expression *at* once, meaning without delay, without hesitation

q: When do you think scientists will find a cure _____ cancer?
e: fixed expression a *cure for* something

q: _____ my opinion, we should not have classes on Fridays.
e: fixed expression *in* someone's opinion

q: When I neared my home, I could see that my neighbor's house was _____ fire.
e: fixed expression *on fire*

q: I think Capt. Arroyo is _____ love again.
e: fixed expression to be *in love* opposite: to fall *out of love* with someone

q: My father disapproves _____ most of my friends.
e: fixed expression *approve of disapprove of*

q: Do you believe _____ ghosts?
e: fixed expression You *believe in* something.

q: I am disappointed _____ you!
e: fixed expression *disappointed in* but *proud of*

q: Musicians have to spend most of their time _____ the road.
e: fixed expression Traveling *on* the road by bus or car or van.

q: I am sick _____ all the political ads on TV.
e: fixed expression to be sick *of* something

q: I would never run _____ political office.
e: fixed expression to run for an office or position

q: My country has been involved _____ wars for most of this century.
e: fixed expression You are *involved in* something.

q: I did it _____ purpose.
e: fixed expression You do something *on* purpose.

q: Water is composed _____ hydrogen and oxygen.
e: fixed expression *composed of*

q: I am very good _____ tennis.
e: fixed expression You are *good at* something or *bad at* something.

q: We need to dispense _____ these exercises for now.
e: fixed expression You *dispoense with* something.

q: What you did is _____ the law.
e: fixed expression *against the law* = illegal *within the law* = legal

q: My neighbor was convicted _____ car theft.
e: Fixed expression to be *convicted of* First, he was *charged with* the crime.

q: Don't brag _____ your accomplishments. Let other people do that.
e: fixed expression You *brag about* something. But you can *boast of* or *boast about* it.

q: I am ashamed _____ myself.
e: fixed expression. Ashamed of. Opposite is proud of.

q: I am feeling down _____ the dumps today.
e: idiom *in* the dumps, because it's a place

q: She is not supposed to do any heavy lifting because she is now _____child.
e: fixed expression *with* child means pregnant.

q: I give up! You are _____ redemption!
e: *Beyond* means past the point of. Fixed expressions: beyond hope, beyond redemption, beyond salvation.

q: I shudder _____ the thought of giving a speech at the graduation dinner.
e: fixed expression You shudder *at* something.

q: I think I'll take a stab _____ learning French next semester.
e: idiom You take a stab *at* doing something.

q: If I tell you a secret, will you promise to keep it _____ strictest confidence?
e: fixed expression to keep *in* confidence

q: Mr. Barrow hit the century mark yesterday.
o: He fired a lot of shots.
He ate and drank too much.
e: hit the mark idiom: to be very accurate. Her criticism really hit the mark.

q: It's time to *hit the hay*.
e: *Hit the hay* = go to bed. In the old days, people slept on piles of hay.

q: I wish Craig wouldn't *hit the bottle* so much.
e: to hit the bottle = to drink alcohol (booze)

q: A person who is broke does not have any _____.
e: idiom to be *broke* = no money

q: I'm tired _____ studying every night.
e: fixed expression *to be tired of* something

q: I'm broke.
e: idiom to be broke = to have no money

q: I told you a little white lie.
e: A *little white lie* = a small lie that is not serious = a *fib*.

q: Prepositions are difficult _____ me to understand.
e: fixed expression Something is difficult or easy *for* a person.

q: _____ fire, do not try to use the elevators.
e: fixed expression meaning "if it should happen." *In case of* rain, the game will be postponed. In case of an emergency, call 911.

q: I am not interested _____ studying English.
e: fixed expression: *to be interested in* something

q: Craig is going to tie the knot next month. What will Craig do?
e: "To tie the knot" is an idiom meaning to get married.

q: That picture is going to cost you *two grand*.
e: a grand = slang term for a thousand dollars *five grand* = $5,000

q: If Craig is going to *hit the slopes* next weekend, what will he do?
e: *Hit the slopes* = ski down the mountainsides

q: The new mechanic was warned that anyone who doesn't *pull their weight* will be moved to the night shift.
o: do a fair share of the work
e: Pull your weight = do your fair share of the work in a team.

q: When the audit found errors, the supervisor *threw his assistant under the bus* to save his own job.
o: let his assistant take the blame
sent his assistant on a long trip
e: Throw someone under the bus = blame or sacrifice someone, often a colleague, to protect yourself.

q: Before we brief the colonel, let's meet for ten minutes so we're all *on the same page*.
e: On the same page = sharing the same understanding of a situation or agreeing on what to do.

q: Having worked at a supply depot before, the new logistics officer was able to *start working effectively from her very first day*.
o: bite off more than she could chew
e: Hit the ground running = start a new job or activity quickly and successfully, with no slow start.

q: The new inspector does everything *by the book*, so expect him to check every item on the list.
o: as quickly as he possibly can
in a relaxed and friendly way
e: By the book = exactly according to the rules and regulations.

q: He's only been in the unit for a week, so *cut him some slack* if he gets lost on base.
o: don't be too hard on him
e: Cut someone some slack = be less strict or critical with someone because of their situation.

q: Repairing all twelve vehicles before Friday's inspection is going to be *something very difficult to achieve*.
e: A tall order = a task or request that is very difficult to do. (A piece of cake = very easy; a done deal = already settled; small potatoes = unimportant.)

q: Lieutenant Moore missed two weeks of planning, so the staff spent the morning bringing her *up to speed*.
o: back to her full physical fitness
ready to lead the convoy at higher speed
in line for an early promotion
e: Bring someone up to speed = give someone the latest information so they understand the current situation.

q: Because of budget cuts, the plan to renovate the base gym has been put *on the back burner*.
e: On the back burner = postponed or given low priority: not canceled, but nobody is working on it now.

q: Between night classes and twelve-hour shifts, Corporal Reyes has been *working too hard and sleeping too little* for months.
o: burning the candle at both ends
e: Burn the candle at both ends = work from early morning until late at night, so you get too little rest.

q: When the shipment went missing, every office tried to *pass the buck* instead of solving the problem.
e: Pass the buck = shift the responsibility or blame to someone else. ("The buck stops here" = I accept final responsibility.)

q: After the company lost its biggest contract, several engineers decided to *leave and go to work for a competitor*.
e: Jump ship = suddenly leave an organization or team, often to join another one.

q: The internship with the defense contractor paid very little, but it helped her *get her foot in the door*.
o: get a first chance in that field
find a cheaper place to live
get through the security gate faster
e: Get your foot in the door = get a first opportunity in an organization or career that can lead to more.

q: Sorry I didn't answer your email — I've been *snowed under* since the audit started.
o: stuck at home by bad weather
away from the office on leave
e: Snowed under = having so much work that you can hardly deal with it.

q: When his wife lost her job, Sergeant Kim took a weekend job to help the family *pay for the basic things it needed*.
e: Make ends meet = have just enough money to pay for food, rent and other basic needs.

q: If you wait until December to book your flight home, you'll *pay through the nose* for it.
e: Pay through the nose = pay much more than something should cost.

q: A weekend in San Antonio won't *break the bank* if we stay at the base lodging.
e: Not break the bank = not cost too much; be affordable.

q: The battalion has agreed to *pay for* the team's hotel rooms during the competition.
e: Foot the bill (for) = pay for something. Do not confuse it with "fit the bill" = be suitable.

q: We've been *pinching pennies* all year so we can afford a trip to see my parents in Ohio.
e: Pinch pennies = be very careful with money and spend as little as possible.

q: By investing a little from every paycheck, Chief Morris built a nice *nest egg* for his retirement.
e: Nest egg = an amount of money saved for the future, especially for retirement.

q: The base bowling alley has been *in the red* for three years, so it may close next spring.
e: In the red = losing money or in debt. The opposite is "in the black" (making a profit).

q: In many military families today, both spouses *earn the money that pays the household bills*.
e: Bring home the bacon = earn the money that supports a family. (Rule the roost = be the boss at home; keep up with the Joneses = try to own as much as the neighbors.)

q: The soldiers' theater club put on the whole show *on a shoestring*, using costumes from their own closets.
e: On a shoestring (budget) = with very little money.

q: I'd love to join you on the ski trip, but I'm *short of money* until payday.
e: Strapped for cash = having very little money at the moment. (Rolling in dough / made of money = very rich.)

q: The new cold-weather jackets at the PX are *selling like hotcakes*.
e: Sell like hotcakes = sell very quickly and in large numbers.

q: For a big airline, a $5,000 fine is *chump change*.
e: Chump change = an amount of money too small to matter to the person or company mentioned.

q: Three restaurants near the main gate *went out of business* during the pandemic.
e: Go belly up = fail completely; go bankrupt (like a dead fish floating upside down).

q: The medevac helicopter arrived *in the nick of time*; the injured hiker had already lost a lot of blood.
o: just before it was too late
in the middle of the night
e: In the nick of time = at the last possible moment, just before it is too late.

q: The deal to keep the factory open was signed *at the last possible moment*, only hours before the deadline.
o: at the drop of a hat
e: At the eleventh hour = at the last possible moment before a deadline.

q: During the flood, engineers worked *around the clock* to keep the pumps running.
e: Around the clock = 24 hours a day, without stopping.

q: Sorry to ask you *with so little warning*, but could you cover my guard shift tonight?
o: in the heat of the moment
e: On short notice = with very little warning or time to prepare.

q: Our flight was delayed four hours, so we *killed time* by walking around the airport shops.
e: Kill time = do something to make the time pass while you wait.

q: The inspection is on Monday, so this weekend is *the critical period when everyone must work hardest*.
e: Crunch time = the critical period, usually just before a deadline, when you must work hardest.

q: We can't afford new radios this year, but we might upgrade them *down the road*.
e: Down the road = at some time in the future.

q: Sergeant Lee is the kind of person who will volunteer *instantly and without any hesitation*.
o: at the drop of a hat
by the skin of his teeth
e: At the drop of a hat = immediately, without hesitating or needing to be asked twice.

q: I'm a little *pressed for time* this morning; can we discuss the schedule after lunch?
e: Pressed for time = in a hurry; without much time available.

q: The rear guard's mission was to slow the enemy down and *gain extra time* for the main column to withdraw.
e: Buy time = delay something so that you have more time. (Kill time = pass time while waiting; make time = find time for something; do time = serve a prison sentence.)

q: The main gym is closed for repairs, so *for the time being* please use the fitness center on the east side.
e: For the time being = for now; temporarily, until something changes.

q: The hard drive crashed and there was no backup, so we had to rebuild the database *from scratch*.
e: From scratch = from the very beginning, without using anything prepared earlier.

q: Getting a slot at Ranger School this year is *a long shot*, but Private Hale plans to apply anyway.
e: A long shot = something that has only a small chance of succeeding.

q: Just after signing up for another four years, Sergeant Ortiz began to *doubt whether he had made the right decision*.
o: have the time of his life
e: Have second thoughts = start to doubt a decision you have made or are about to make.

q: When you can't decide between two good job offers, sometimes you just have to *go with your gut*.
e: Go with your gut = follow your instinct or feeling instead of long analysis.

q: The new body armor is lighter, but *the jury is still out* on whether it actually offers better protection.
e: The jury is still out (on something) = people have not yet reached a decision or opinion about it.

q: After renting for ten years, Mike and Dana finally *made the big decision* and bought a house near the base.
e: Take the plunge = finally decide to do something important or risky after thinking about it for a long time.

q: Free college tuition in exchange for two more years of service? For me, that was *a no-brainer*.
e: A no-brainer = a decision so easy and obvious that you hardly need to think about it.

q: Both teams in the base basketball final are equally strong, so the game is *impossible to predict*.
e: A toss-up = a situation where either result is equally likely, like tossing a coin.

q: Captain Wells had planned to retire, but she *had a change of heart* and signed up for another tour.
e: Have a change of heart = change your opinion or decision about something.

q: When drones became popular, dozens of small companies *joined the trend just because it was fashionable*.
o: jumped through a lot of hoops
e: Jump on the bandwagon = join something because it is popular, not because you really believe in it. (Jump the gun = act too soon.)

q: My financial advisor warned me not to *put all my eggs in one basket*.
e: Put all your eggs in one basket = risk everything on a single plan or investment.

q: The weather forecast was uncertain, but the commander decided to *be extra careful* and cancel the night jump.
o: err on the side of caution
e: Err on the side of caution = choose the safer option when you are not sure. (Throw caution to the wind = take a big risk.)

q: After the prototype failed three field tests, the Army *pulled the plug on* the whole project.
e: Pull the plug on something = stop a project or activity, often by ending its funding.

q: We can argue about the details all day, but *the bottom line* is that the job must be finished by Friday.
o: the last line of the report
e: The bottom line = the most important fact, or the final result (from the last line of a financial statement).
